source: When we last left Ophelia, she was ready to use the Book of Fates to hold off Fortinbras' invasion and save everyone's lives.
S-so she did it! She's saved us all from a tragic fate!
Ah... so it would seem.
I for one am thrilled to not be the only one left alive.
As much as you're all a group of rather moody, melodramatic fools, you've become my melodramatic fools.
I did not think I would live long enough to spend all the money I made fleecing the guards out of their pay.
What a relief it is to be proven wrong.
And I'm sure you'll steal a lot more of their pay before you go to your grave kicking, old woman.
Yes, or until they grow wiser about my loaded dice. I'm sure I'll die before that happens. Idiots.
At one point, I wanted nothing more than to die.
Now the gift of life is thrust upon us.
Even those of us who didn't deserve to live are here.
Stop that, Hamlet.
It's true you and your uncle have been at odds lately. However...
Now that the war is won, there is time for peace to come to us all, in our own ways, in our own time!
Yes, we ought to celebrate this gift of peace we've all been given!
Your Highness... the war is not won.
Did you think the war was over?
It... it isn't?
No. Of course it isn't.
Fortinbras may have been stopped for now, but he is relentless, and his men are brutally faithful to him.
They will come for him. And when he is free, they will come for our country.
But we are well prepared. I've rallied good men to my side. Useful men.
Let us give them a fight worth fighting!
This won't be a fight. It'll be a slow massacre.
Only a war of attrition lies ahead.
What she speaks is truth, my lord. Fortinbras will not relent. And neither shall we.
The men we have rallied are sufficient, but not a force worth marveling at. I predict weary years ahead.
We averted a coup. We have not won a war.
Then we shall all bear witness to whatever mysteries the future brings.
I suppose we cannot truly know. Not yet.
That is the summary of it, yes.
Consider your options carefully, Ophelia.
Life in place of death is not always a gift. You and I know that truest of all.
When we last left Ophelia, she was ready to use the Book of Fates to marry Prince Hamlet and become Queen of Denmark.
What say you all about this?
Excellent. Good riddance to both of you.
And a special thanks to you, Ophelia. You've saved me from a life of having to be near Hamlet.
Evidently my mood of late was more offensive to all of you than I thought.
Happens to the best of us, Hamlet. But it seems as though this betrothal has turned your state around.
Much as I hate to admit it, I've never seen you happier.
I suppose... it's changed me.
Everyone, I must apologize for my mood as of late.
It's been the darkest year of my life. There were moments when I prayed for death more fervently than I've ever wanted anything.
But... Ophelia showed me a world where it was possible to reclaim who I was before.
The old me wasn't gone. He was merely buried under the weight of paralyzing fear.
And I'm no longer afraid.
Especially with you by my side.
This was the union I always desired.
I merely wish it had happened sooner. But...
Well, circumstances were different then.
I am, and shall always be, opposed to this union.
We know Polonius's estate is dry. No dowry to her name, no social ties, no status... it weakens Denmark.
A King ought to marry strategically. Not on his own blind whim!
Hush, brother.
This world belongs to the living.
We are merely passing through, here only for this singular moment in time.
Ophelia. Would that I could offer you the embrace of love a father-in-law ought to have for his daughter.
My son... the darkness which unfolded within him in these past months has been buried, but not truly forgotten.
And someday, it shall rise up again to lash against you both.
Can you be prepared for that eternity? Can you love him despite that, knowing it has hurt you before?
Think on that before you decide his fate, and yours.
And then there's Father and I. He exiled us, Ophelia.
He'd kill us if he could.
Try as you might, you won't change his heart on this front. He knows I'm a danger to him. And he's right. I'll never serve him as my King.
You will grow old without either of us in your life.
Do Father and I mean so little to you that you're willing to throw us away?
When we last left Ophelia, she was ready to use the Book of Fates to allow Norway to rule through Hamlet, bringing the two countries into a partnership of sorts.
Is this not the world any decent person would seek? A world where all survive?
One where Hamlet is free to take his father's throne, and forced by virtue of another ruler to act, rather than remain paralyzed?
Certainly I think so.
W-well, what about me? Where is my life in all this?
Ophelia, have you deemed me beyond redemption? Am I not included in your salvation?
Feh! Should've considered that before you offed a perfectly good king!
Look at the mess you made of it all!
The mess I've made? What of Denmark? What of our nation?
We're scarcely our own people now. Merely a pale shadow of Norway's ambitions.
And what shall become of Denmark in a dozen years, or in a hundred? Shall we even exist?
All of our stories, all of our selves forgotten!
Have all of you forgotten Ogier, that knight of Charlemagne? Legend says his spirit dwells within this very castle.
And when Denmark is most at peril, he shall rise and take arms to defend us all. Have you forgotten what others sacrificed?
It is the King of Denmark's calling to fight on her behalf. What kind of coward merely hands her over to her enemies?
An entire nation's identity must not be snuffed out by the whims of a boy!
Claudius is not wrong.
But of all foreign rulers, I think my husband respected Fortinbras and his family as the greatest.
Is that true, Hamlet?
Indeed. You always knew my heart best, Gerta.
At the same time...
I am certainly not proud to lose everything I spent my life fighting for.
I wish my son were strong enough to stand and fight.
As do I, Father.
I fear I shall think of that every morning until you and I can discuss it at length in Heaven one day.
We mustn't be too hard on Hamlet.
A war with Fortinbras would have cost more than any of us know.
I cannot say whether we would have won. But the destruction would have been... extensive.
Many would have died to keep Denmark as Denmark.
Ophelia, you're trading away a nation to keep people alive.
My father would not have made that trade. Claudius would not. Neither would King Hamlet.
...Nor, truthfully, can I claim that I would, either.
But you aren't like any of us. That's why you were able to keep all of us alive.
Just be careful. Be careful what you're willing to give up. Know that it cannot be recovered.
Ah. You're here. Come. Have a seat.
What're you having?
No wine tonight. I think this calls for some of that aqua vitae you keep in the back.
I didn't come here to drink.
Of course you did. You just don't know it yet. Once more: Have a seat.
I think you already suspect what this is about, don't you?
I spend quite a lot of time in town. And I've seen you around quite often, too.
I... I don't know why I came.
You should thank Ophelia for getting us together. It was her doing.
I've seen your performances, you know. Several times. You have talent.
There are times when player and part align, and the human being onstage truly becomes their character...
When the performer leaves the stage, it's impossible for me to see them as anything other than the person they played. It is the ultimate resonance.
So I shall leave it to you to tell me. What part of your heart is Bernardo, and what part of you is someone else?
How can you ask me that?
I cannot know that.
I think you do.
And I think you're afraid, because you know the answer will change your world greatly.
Let me tell you a story, my friend, whomever you are.
I was raised in Italy. When my father passed, I made my way to Florence seeking work.
There, I found a world of creation. Every small building held an artist's workshop, it seemed. Every street was full of music.
I stumbled into one of these workshops once, and became an assistant to a great artist. He painted human beings as I'd never seen them.
I learned that human bodies were—not dirty and sinful, as my father once had me believe, but full of light. Beautiful and wondrous.
And there... I learned about what the French call the 'Italian vice.'
I fell in love with my master, and he with me. He taught me that love-making, like painting, is an art form unto itself.
In Florence, love between men is common. The Germans call a man like me Florenzer. I never thought it strange.
It was only upon coming here, to Denmark, that I realized the rest of the world treats these matters as sinful.
An... entire city of sodomites? Surely God will smite Florence for such wickedness.
Ah. You see, that's the curious thing.
Upon leaving Florence, I felt compelled to travel to see that little chapel Michelangelo painted. I'd heard it was rather a nice work of his.
Looking up into the face of the Christian God, reaching out to touch Man... I realized.
Your God is pure, infinite love. A love for humankind which surpasses even the stars. How could he ever hate his own creation?
How could a being of such magnificence ever turn upon the thing he had created in his own image?
So when you came to Elsinore, you hid your preference for men.
I did. For my own safety. It was simple: There is only one Dane worth loving at the moment, and he is thoroughly unavailable to me.
You mustn't think of it like some sad, one-sided, pining-away sort of thing, though. I love him in a number of ways.
Above all, he is my dearest, truest friend-- though he might be going through the darkest time of his life right now.
I wanted to see his grief through to its sticking place. I'll leave Elsinore and return to Italy very soon, I expect.
I did. For my own safety. It was simple: There was only ever one Dane worth loving at the moment, and he was thoroughly unavailable to me.
